title: 25 Jun 2025
des: Oman Pearson VUE paediatrics recall, 25 June 2025. Answers checked and explained.

questions.question: Which of the following most increases the risk of respiratory distress syndrome (hyaline membrane disease) in a preterm baby?
questions.exp: Maternal diabetes delays surfactant maturation, because fetal hyperinsulinaemia blocks the effect of cortisol on type II pneumocytes, so infants of diabetic mothers get RDS even near term. Maternal opiate (heroin) use, prolonged rupture of membranes, intrauterine stress and Black ethnicity are all linked to a LOWER risk of RDS. Other risk factors: prematurity, male sex, caesarean section without labour, second twin and perinatal asphyxia.

questions.question: A child with poor growth has a normal creatinine, serum bicarbonate 15 mmol/L and a urine pH of 8.5. Which serum value is most likely to be low?
questions.exp: A normal anion gap metabolic acidosis with an inappropriately alkaline urine (pH above 5.5) is distal (type 1) renal tubular acidosis. The distal tubule cannot secrete H+, so more K+ is lost instead, giving hypokalaemia. Chloride is HIGH (hyperchloraemic acidosis). Calcium is usually normal in serum, but hypercalciuria causes nephrocalcinosis and stones. Treatment is oral alkali (citrate or bicarbonate).

questions.question: A 12-month-old boy was born at 32 weeks' gestation. He sits without support, pulls to stand using the furniture, says "baba" and "mama" and has a pincer grasp. Which statement about his gross motor development is true?
questions.a: He has a mild delay, one standard deviation below the mean
questions.b: He is behind in gross motor development
questions.c: It is normal for his corrected age
questions.d: He is behind in language development
questions.e: He is behind in fine motor development
questions.exp: Correct for prematurity until 2 years of age: 12 months minus 8 weeks early = a corrected age of about 10 months. Sitting without support (6–8 months), pulling to stand (9–10 months), pincer grasp (9–10 months) and "mama/baba" babble (9–10 months) are all normal for 10 months.

questions.question: What is the most common congenital heart defect in children?
questions.exp: VSD is the most common congenital heart lesion (about 30% of all CHD, excluding bicuspid aortic valve). Tetralogy of Fallot is the most common cyanotic lesion after the neonatal period, and transposition of the great arteries is the most common cyanotic lesion presenting in the newborn.

questions.question: A ventilated term neonate has a mean airway pressure of 15 cmH2O, FiO2 0.8 and PaO2 60 mmHg. What is the oxygenation index?
questions.exp: Oxygenation index = (mean airway pressure x FiO2 x 100) / PaO2 = (15 x 0.8 x 100) / 60 = 20. Higher OI means more severe respiratory failure: OI above 25 is severe hypoxaemic failure (consider inhaled nitric oxide), and OI above 40 is a usual threshold for ECMO.

questions.question: A new test is used on 200 children who are known to have a disease. It is positive in 180 of them. What is the sensitivity of the test?
questions.b: It cannot be worked out without the number of healthy children
questions.exp: Sensitivity = true positives / all with the disease = 180 / 200 = 90%. Sensitivity only needs the diseased group; specificity (true negatives / all without the disease) would need the healthy group, and predictive values need both groups plus the prevalence.

questions.question: In a trial, 20% of children in the control group and 15% in the treatment group develop the outcome. What is the number needed to treat?
questions.exp: Absolute risk reduction = 20% − 15% = 5% (0.05). NNT = 1 / ARR = 1 / 0.05 = 20: twenty children must be treated to prevent one outcome. The relative risk reduction is 5/20 = 25%.

questions.question: Which study design best shows a causal relationship between a treatment and its outcome?
questions.exp: Randomisation balances known and unknown confounders, so a difference in outcome can be attributed to the treatment. The RCT is the strongest single-study design for cause and effect (systematic reviews of RCTs rank above it). Case–control studies suit rare diseases, cross-sectional studies measure prevalence, and case series only describe.

questions.question: A 3-day-old baby has bilateral purulent conjunctivitis with marked eyelid swelling. Gram stain shows Gram-negative intracellular diplococci. What is the treatment?
questions.b: A single dose of intramuscular or intravenous ceftriaxone
questions.exp: Conjunctivitis on days 2–5 with heavy purulent discharge is gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum, which can perforate the cornea. Give a single dose of ceftriaxone 25–50 mg/kg (max 125 mg) IM/IV, irrigate the eyes, admit, and test and treat the mother and partner (also for chlamydia). Topical treatment alone is not enough. Chlamydial conjunctivitis (days 5–14) is treated with oral erythromycin for 14 days.

questions.question: A baby born at 29 weeks has ROP screening. There is a flat white demarcation line in zone III of both eyes. What stage of retinopathy of prematurity is this?
questions.exp: ROP stages: 1 = flat demarcation line between vascular and avascular retina; 2 = ridge (the line gains height and width); 3 = ridge with extraretinal fibrovascular proliferation; 4 = partial retinal detachment; 5 = total detachment. Zone III is the outermost temporal crescent; zone III stage 1–2 disease usually regresses and is followed up only.

questions.question: A healthy 4-year-old has a soft grade 2/6 vibratory, musical systolic murmur at the left lower sternal border. It is louder lying down and during a fever. He is well, with normal pulses and a normal second heart sound. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Still's murmur is the most common innocent murmur at 3–6 years: a short, low-pitched, musical (twanging) systolic murmur at the left lower sternal border, louder supine and with fever or exercise. A venous hum is continuous, heard below the clavicles, and disappears when lying flat or turning the neck. Features of innocent murmurs: soft, systolic, short, symptomless, sternal edge, changes with posture, no thrill, normal S2.

questions.question: The same child has a typical innocent murmur. What is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Reassure the parents; no investigation or follow-up is needed
questions.exp: An innocent murmur in a well child needs no tests. Explain that it is a normal flow noise from a normal heart. Refer if there are red flags: diastolic or pansystolic murmur, grade 3 or more or a thrill, abnormal S2, symptoms (poor feeding, breathlessness, syncope), abnormal pulses, or a murmur in a neonate.

questions.question: A 3-year-old has had fever for 6 days, bilateral non-purulent conjunctival injection, red cracked lips, a polymorphous rash, swelling of the hands and feet and a 2 cm unilateral cervical lymph node. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Kawasaki disease: fever for 5 days or more plus 4 of 5 features: bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, oral changes (red cracked lips, strawberry tongue), polymorphous rash, extremity changes (oedema/erythema, later peeling), and a cervical lymph node 1.5 cm or more (usually unilateral). The main risk is coronary artery aneurysm, so do an echocardiogram.

questions.question: A child is diagnosed with Kawasaki disease on day 6 of fever. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.exp: IVIG 2 g/kg as a single infusion over 10–12 hours, ideally within 10 days of fever onset, cuts coronary aneurysms from about 25% to under 5%. Add aspirin (moderate to high dose until afebrile, then low dose 3–5 mg/kg/day for 6–8 weeks, or longer if there are aneurysms). Steroids are added for high-risk disease; infliximab or a second IVIG dose for resistant disease.

questions.question: A child with Kawasaki disease and a coronary artery aneurysm is discharged on long-term low-dose aspirin. Which recommendation should be given?
questions.b: Give the inactivated influenza vaccine every year
questions.c: Stop the aspirin as soon as the fever settles
questions.d: Avoid all live vaccines for life
questions.e: Give a further dose of IVIG every month
questions.exp: Children on long-term aspirin are at risk of Reye syndrome if they catch influenza or varicella, so they need an annual inactivated influenza vaccine (and varicella vaccination when allowed). Live vaccines (MMR, varicella) are delayed for 11 months after IVIG because the antibodies stop them working, but they are not banned for life.

questions.question: A child had hives after eating egg. Which advice is correct about the influenza vaccine?
questions.a: Give half the dose, then the other half 30 minutes later
questions.c: Give the vaccine only after skin-prick testing with the vaccine
questions.d: Give it only in hospital with a 2-hour observation period
questions.e: Give the influenza vaccine as normal
questions.exp: Egg allergy, including severe allergy and anaphylaxis, is no longer a contraindication to influenza vaccines. The egg (ovalbumin) content is tiny, so egg-allergic children are vaccinated in the usual setting with the usual observation. No skin testing or split dosing is needed. (Previous anaphylaxis to the vaccine itself is a contraindication.)

questions.question: A 4-day-old baby presents with lethargy, poor feeding and reduced activity. Blood gas: pH 7.54, pCO2 18 mmHg (2.4 kPa), HCO3 21 mmol/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: A sick neonate with a respiratory alkalosis (high pH, low pCO2, near-normal bicarbonate) suggests hyperammonaemia, which drives the respiratory centre: think of a urea cycle defect such as OTC deficiency (X-linked, the most common). Organic acidaemias (methylmalonic, propionic) and MSUD cause a metabolic ACIDOSIS with a high anion gap. PKU does not present acutely in the newborn. Check ammonia urgently.

questions.question: A child has had meningococcal meningitis twice. Which immune defect is most likely?
questions.e: Classical complement pathway deficiency (C1, C2, C4)
questions.exp: Deficiency of the terminal complement components (C5–C9, the membrane attack complex) or properdin causes recurrent Neisseria infections (meningococcus, gonococcus). Screen with CH50 and AH50. Early classical pathway deficiency (C1q, C2, C4) causes SLE-like disease and encapsulated bacterial infections. Vaccinate against meningococcus (ACWY and B).

questions.question: A 1-year-old boy has right ear discharge. On examination the tonsils are absent. He has had Haemophilus influenzae pneumonia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: XLA (Bruton tyrosine kinase defect) causes absent B cells and very low immunoglobulins. Boys present after 6 months, when maternal IgG has gone, with recurrent infections by encapsulated bacteria (otitis, sinusitis, pneumonia). Lymphoid tissue (tonsils, adenoids, lymph nodes) is absent or tiny. Treatment is lifelong immunoglobulin replacement.

questions.question: A 2-week-old baby has cyanosis and breathlessness. There is a left parasternal heave and a single loud second heart sound with no murmur. The chest X-ray shows a small heart with marked pulmonary venous congestion. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.a: Obstructed total anomalous pulmonary venous return
questions.exp: Obstructed (usually infracardiac) TAPVR presents early with severe cyanosis and respiratory distress, a right ventricular heave, a loud single S2 and often no murmur. The X-ray shows a normal-sized or small heart with a white-out or venous congestion pattern. It is a surgical emergency. ToF, pulmonary atresia and tricuspid atresia have REDUCED pulmonary flow (oligaemic lungs); myocarditis gives a large heart.

questions.question: A 2-month-old has cough and fever of 39°C. Heart rate is 185/min, there are bilateral crackles and the liver is 4 cm below the costal margin. Which drug should be given first?
questions.exp: Tachycardia, tachypnoea, crackles and hepatomegaly in an infant mean congestive heart failure (consider myocarditis or a large left-to-right shunt). First-line treatment is a diuretic (furosemide) to relieve fluid overload, with oxygen and treatment of the cause. Digoxin is rarely first-line now; inotropes such as adrenaline or dopamine are for low cardiac output or shock.

questions.question: A child with HIV has fever, breathlessness and bilateral interstitial infiltrates on chest X-ray. Which antibiotic is best?
questions.exp: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia is the classic AIDS-defining pneumonia: hypoxia out of proportion to signs and bilateral interstitial (ground-glass) infiltrates. Treat with high-dose IV co-trimoxazole for 21 days, adding steroids if hypoxic. Co-trimoxazole is also used as prophylaxis in HIV-exposed and HIV-infected children.

questions.question: A 2-month-old has a squint. On examination the right eye has a white pupillary reflex. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Leukocoria with strabismus in an infant is retinoblastoma until proven otherwise: refer urgently to ophthalmology. It is the most common primary eye cancer in children (RB1 gene, chromosome 13q14); bilateral or familial cases are germline. Congenital cataract also gives a white reflex, but squint plus white reflex is the classic retinoblastoma presentation in exams.

questions.question: A child with cerebral palsy comes in because his gastrostomy tube fell out at home. The stoma is moist, with no sign of infection. What should be done?
questions.a: Leave the stoma covered with a dry dressing
questions.b: Send him home and ask him to come back later
questions.d: Insert a Foley (urinary) catheter into the stoma to keep the tract open
questions.e: Book a surgical review for a new gastrostomy next week
questions.exp: A gastrostomy tract can start to close within 1–2 hours. If a replacement gastrostomy tube is not available, put a Foley catheter (same or smaller size) into the stoma to keep it open until the proper tube is replaced. Do not use it for feeds until the position is confirmed. If the tract is less than about 6 weeks old, call the surgical or endoscopy team, as it may not be mature.

questions.question: A 4-year-old boy presents with carpopedal spasm. Potassium is 3.0 mmol/L, magnesium 0.56 mmol/L and the urine calcium:creatinine ratio is low. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Gitelman syndrome is a defect of the thiazide-sensitive NaCl cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule: hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, HYPOmagnesaemia and HYPOcalciuria. It presents in older children with cramps and tetany. Bartter syndrome (loop of Henle) presents earlier with polyuria and HYPERcalciuria. Liddle syndrome gives hypertension.

questions.question: A 7-year-old girl has episodes of palpitations. Her resting ECG shows a short PR interval and a slurred upstroke of the QRS complex (delta wave). What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: WPW: an accessory pathway (bundle of Kent) causes pre-excitation, with a short PR interval, a delta wave and a wide QRS, plus attacks of re-entrant SVT. Lown–Ganong–Levine has a short PR but no delta wave. Long QT and Brugada cause ventricular arrhythmias rather than pre-excitation.

questions.question: A child has a heart rate of 240/min. After treatment with adenosine, the ECG in sinus rhythm shows a short PR interval and a delta wave. Which drug should be avoided for long-term prevention?
questions.exp: The ECG after cardioversion shows Wolff–Parkinson–White syndrome. Digoxin (and verapamil) slow the AV node and can speed conduction down the accessory pathway, so atrial fibrillation can turn into ventricular fibrillation. Use beta-blockers or flecainide for prevention; catheter ablation is the definitive treatment.

questions.question: An 11-year-old boy has short stature, delayed puberty and a normal growth velocity. His mother had her first period at 14 years. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.a: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty
questions.exp: Constitutional delay: short for age but growing at a normal rate, delayed bone age, late puberty, and often a family history of late puberty (late menarche in the mother or a late growth spurt in the father). Final height is normal for the family. GH deficiency and hypothyroidism give a LOW growth velocity. Familial short stature has a normal bone age and normal timing of puberty.

questions.question: A short boy has undescended testes and a systolic murmur. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Noonan syndrome (PTPN11, autosomal dominant) affects both sexes: short stature, webbed neck, low-set ears, ptosis and hypertelorism, pectus, cryptorchidism, bleeding problems, and pulmonary valve stenosis (systolic murmur) or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Turner syndrome occurs only in phenotypic females. Prader–Willi also has cryptorchidism, but with hypotonia, obesity and no typical heart lesion.

questions.question: A 12-year-old girl grew 7 cm in the past year. She has not started her periods. On examination the breast bud and areola are enlarged, and there is a small amount of hair, mainly along the labia. What is her sexual maturity rating (Tanner stage)?
questions.exp: Breast stage 2 = breast bud with enlargement of the areola. Pubic hair stage 2 = sparse, slightly pigmented hair mainly along the labia. Stage 3 = further enlargement of breast and areola with no separation of contours, and darker, coarser hair spreading over the pubis. Menarche usually comes at stage 4, about 2 years after thelarche.

questions.question: A child with acute lymphoblastic leukaemia on chemotherapy develops leg weakness with reduced reflexes. Which drug is most likely to cause this?
questions.exp: Vincristine causes a dose-related peripheral neuropathy: loss of ankle reflexes, jaw pain, foot drop, constipation (autonomic) and ptosis. Methotrexate causes mucositis and leukoencephalopathy, asparaginase causes pancreatitis, thrombosis and allergy, mercaptopurine causes myelosuppression and liver damage, and daunorubicin causes cardiotoxicity.

questions.question: A child with haemolytic uraemic syndrome has tall peaked T waves and widened QRS complexes on the ECG (hyperkalaemia). What is the first treatment?
questions.exp: Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes is an emergency. First give IV 10% calcium gluconate (0.5 mL/kg over 5–10 minutes) to stabilise the heart muscle; it does not lower potassium. Then shift K+ into cells (nebulised salbutamol, insulin with glucose) and remove it (calcium resonium, dialysis). In anuric HUS, dialysis is often needed.

questions.question: An 8-year-old girl has precocious puberty and hyperthyroidism. She has large hyperpigmented skin patches with jagged edges that do not cross the midline. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: McCune–Albright syndrome (somatic GNAS activating mutation) has a triad: peripheral (GnRH-independent) precocious puberty, café-au-lait patches with irregular "coast of Maine" borders that stop at the midline, and polyostotic fibrous dysplasia. Other endocrine overactivity can occur: hyperthyroidism, GH excess, Cushing syndrome. NF1 café-au-lait spots are smooth ("coast of California").

questions.question: A girl with anorexia nervosa starts refeeding. Which electrolyte abnormality is most characteristic of refeeding syndrome?
questions.exp: When carbohydrate is reintroduced, insulin drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells. Hypophosphataemia is the hallmark and is the most dangerous (falls are greatest in the first 2–5 days). Start feeds cautiously, monitor phosphate, K+, Mg2+ and glucose daily, and give thiamine and phosphate supplements.

questions.question: A malnourished adolescent with anorexia nervosa is refed too quickly. Which serious complication is most likely?
questions.exp: Refeeding syndrome: low phosphate (less ATP), low potassium and magnesium, sodium and water retention, and thiamine deficiency. The starved, thin heart muscle cannot cope with the extra fluid load, so congestive cardiac failure and arrhythmias are the main cause of death. Other features: weakness, respiratory failure, seizures, rhabdomyolysis and Wernicke encephalopathy.

questions.question: A 13-year-old girl who plays a lot of sport has pain and swelling below her left knee during exercise. There is a tender bony lump over the tibial tuberosity and no knee joint effusion. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Osgood–Schlatter disease is a traction apophysitis of the tibial tuberosity in active adolescents during the growth spurt: pain with activity, a tender swelling at the tuberosity and no effusion. Treatment is rest from aggravating sport, ice, analgesia and quadriceps stretching; it settles when growth ends. Night pain, constant pain or systemic features need an X-ray to exclude a tumour.

questions.question: A preterm baby on CPAP develops abdominal distension, bilious aspirates and feed intolerance. The abdominal X-ray shows intramural gas. What is the most likely cause?
questions.exp: Pneumatosis intestinalis (intramural gas) is the radiological sign of NEC (Bell stage II). Stop feeds, insert a gastric tube on free drainage, start broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and parenteral nutrition, and involve the surgeons. Spontaneous intestinal perforation in extremely preterm babies (often after steroids or indomethacin) shows free air without pneumatosis. CPAP belly is simple gaseous distension in a well baby.

questions.question: A 4-day-old baby is well but has a very low platelet count. The mother's platelet count is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.c: Neonatal autoimmune thrombocytopenia from maternal ITP
questions.exp: A well baby with severe thrombocytopenia and a mother with a NORMAL platelet count = NAIT: maternal antibodies against a fetal platelet antigen inherited from the father (usually HPA-1a). It can cause intracranial haemorrhage, even before birth, and can affect a first pregnancy. Give HPA-matched (or random) platelets with or without IVIG. In maternal ITP the mother's platelets are low. A sick baby suggests sepsis or DIC.

questions.question: A girl presents in the first months of life with infantile spasms. Brain imaging shows absent corpus callosum, and eye examination shows chorioretinal lacunae. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Aicardi syndrome (X-linked dominant, lethal in males, so seen in girls): triad of infantile spasms, agenesis of the corpus callosum and chorioretinal lacunae, with severe developmental delay. Rett syndrome (MECP2) causes regression after normal early development, with hand-wringing.

questions.question: A 2-week-old baby born at home, with poor antenatal care, presents with seizures needing midazolam. The umbilical stump oozes blood easily when touched by the nappy. Cranial ultrasound shows an intracranial haemorrhage. What is the most likely cause?
questions.c: Vitamin K deficiency bleeding (haemorrhagic disease of the newborn)
questions.exp: Babies born at home often miss vitamin K at birth. Late vitamin K deficiency bleeding (2–12 weeks, mostly breastfed babies) often presents with intracranial haemorrhage, plus umbilical, gut or skin bleeding. PT is very prolonged; platelets and fibrinogen are normal. Give IV vitamin K and fresh frozen plasma or prothrombin complex. Prevent it with 1 mg IM vitamin K at birth.

questions.question: A 4-year-old boy has multiple enlarged cervical lymph nodes, fever, and swelling of the eyelids and face. Full blood count and electrolytes are normal. What should be done next?
questions.b: Start oral antibiotics and review in 2 weeks
questions.d: Reassure; reactive lymph nodes are common at this age
questions.e: Lymph node biopsy under general anaesthesia
questions.exp: Facial and eyelid swelling with lymphadenopathy suggests superior vena cava obstruction from a mediastinal mass (lymphoma, T-cell ALL). A chest X-ray comes first: an anterior mediastinal mass makes sedation or general anaesthesia dangerous (airway and vascular collapse), so the tissue diagnosis must be planned with that in mind (pleural fluid, peripheral blood, or biopsy under local anaesthetic).

questions.question: A 2-week-old baby has peeling skin on the palms, a skin rash and low platelets. What is the proper treatment?
questions.exp: Desquamation of the palms and soles, a rash, snuffles, hepatosplenomegaly and thrombocytopenia are features of early congenital syphilis. Treatment is aqueous crystalline benzylpenicillin 50,000 units/kg IV every 12 hours (every 8 hours after day 7) for 10 days (10–14 days in many guides). Check maternal and infant non-treponemal titres, and do a lumbar puncture, long-bone X-rays and an eye check.

questions.question: A 7-month-old boy has a high fever and is irritable but feeding well and not toxic. Urine culture grows more than 100,000 E. coli per mL. What is the best plan?
questions.a: A single dose of intramuscular gentamicin only
questions.b: No antibiotics until the sensitivity result is back
questions.d: Oral antibiotics at home with follow-up
questions.e: Admit for observation and oral antibiotics
questions.exp: For infants over 3 months with an upper UTI (pyelonephritis) who are not seriously ill and can feed and take medicine, oral antibiotics (such as cefalexin or co-amoxiclav) for 7–10 days work as well as IV treatment. Admit for IV antibiotics if under 3 months, seriously ill or septic, vomiting or unable to take oral medicine, or if there is no response within 48 hours.

questions.question: A 2-month-old infant recovers well from a first pyelonephritis with a typical E. coli and a quick response to antibiotics. What is the best follow-up imaging?
questions.exp: For a first typical UTI under 6 months that responds within 48 hours, NICE recommends a renal and bladder ultrasound (within 6 weeks). DMSA (for scarring, 4–6 months later) and MCUG (for reflux) are added for atypical or recurrent UTIs. CT and IVU are not used.

questions.question: A boy has generalised oedema. Tests show proteinuria and a high triglyceride level. Which test should be done next to confirm nephrotic-range proteinuria?
questions.exp: Nephrotic syndrome = heavy proteinuria (early-morning urine protein:creatinine ratio over 200 mg/mmol, or 3+ on dipstick), low albumin (under 25 g/L) and oedema; high lipids are common. The spot UPCR replaces 24-hour urine collection in children. Renal biopsy is NOT needed in typical steroid-sensitive nephrotic syndrome (age 1–12, normal BP and complement); it is for steroid resistance or atypical features.

questions.question: An adolescent girl dies in the emergency department after resuscitation. How should the family be told?
questions.a: Ask the nurse to tell them
questions.b: Ask them to wait and speak to them later
questions.c: Tell them in the corridor straight away
questions.d: Tell them by telephone after they go home
questions.e: A senior doctor meets the parents in a private room, sits down and tells them clearly that she has died
questions.exp: Breaking bad news: the senior clinician who knows the facts should speak, with a nurse present, in a quiet private room, sitting down, without interruptions. Give a warning shot, use plain words ("died", not euphemisms), allow silence and questions, and offer to let them see their child and contact support (bereavement, faith). Do not delegate it or make the family wait without information.

questions.question: A child with asthma comes to the emergency department unable to complete sentences. She has already had nebulised salbutamol and a steroid with no improvement. What should be given next?
questions.exp: Severe acute asthma not responding to repeated bronchodilators (salbutamol plus ipratropium) and steroids: give IV magnesium sulphate 40 mg/kg (max 2 g) over 20 minutes, then consider IV salbutamol or aminophylline and call the intensive care team. Sedation is contraindicated, and antibiotics are not routinely needed.

questions.question: A 7-year-old with asthma uses a low-dose inhaled corticosteroid (fluticasone 125 micrograms/day) correctly but still has frequent symptoms. According to GINA (2019), what is the next step?
questions.c: Add a long-acting beta-agonist, or increase to a medium-dose inhaled corticosteroid
questions.e: Stop the inhaled steroid and use salbutamol only
questions.exp: First check adherence, inhaler technique and triggers. For children 6–11 years not controlled on low-dose ICS (step 2), GINA step 3 is low-dose ICS-LABA or medium-dose ICS (a leukotriene receptor antagonist is another option). Oral steroids and biologics belong to steps 4–5, after specialist review.

questions.question: A well 2-week-old baby has an annular red rash on the face (around the eyes), neck and trunk. The heart rate is 70/min. What is the most likely cause?
questions.exp: Neonatal lupus comes from maternal anti-Ro (SSA) and anti-La (SSB) antibodies crossing the placenta. It gives an annular, scaly rash on the face (periorbital "raccoon eyes"), scalp and trunk, made worse by sunlight, and congenital complete heart block (slow heart rate), which is permanent. The rash fades by 6 months. Check maternal antibodies, an ECG and a pacing assessment; many mothers have no symptoms.

questions.question: A 2-day-old baby has bilious vomiting, a distended abdomen and has not passed meconium. On rectal examination the rectum is empty and is followed by an explosive gush of stool and gas. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Hirschsprung disease (absent ganglion cells in the distal bowel) presents with delayed meconium (beyond 48 hours), distension and bilious vomiting; the rectum feels empty and tight, and a "blast sign" follows the examination. Diagnose with a suction rectal biopsy. Duodenal atresia gives early vomiting with a scaphoid abdomen and a double bubble. Meconium ileus is linked to cystic fibrosis.

questions.question: An antenatal scan at 22 weeks shows a lethal skeletal dysplasia with severe rib and limb changes. The parents want to continue the pregnancy. When should the palliative care team be involved?
questions.c: There is no need for palliative care referral
questions.e: Only if the baby survives the first week
questions.exp: Perinatal palliative care should start as soon as a life-limiting condition is diagnosed antenatally. Early involvement allows a birth plan, decisions about resuscitation, comfort care, memory-making and family support. Waiting until birth leaves no time to plan.

questions.question: A child has fever, bone pain, aches and headache. Blood count shows lymphopenia, and blood cultures grow small Gram-negative coccobacilli. Which history is most likely?
questions.b: Recent travel to a dengue area
questions.exp: Brucellosis (Brucella melitensis) is caught from unpasteurised milk and dairy products or contact with goats, sheep and camels; it is common in the Middle East. Fever (often undulant), sweats, arthralgia, bone pain and sacroiliitis, hepatosplenomegaly. Blood culture (slow, small Gram-negative coccobacilli) and serology. Treat children over 8 with doxycycline plus rifampicin (or gentamicin); under 8, co-trimoxazole plus rifampicin, for at least 6 weeks.

questions.question: A teenage girl washes her hands many times a day and checks things repeatedly. The thoughts distress her and she knows they are excessive. Which drug is the treatment of choice?
questions.d: A selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (such as sertraline or fluoxetine)
questions.exp: Obsessive–compulsive disorder: first-line treatment is cognitive behavioural therapy with exposure and response prevention. If symptoms are moderate to severe or CBT is not enough, add an SSRI (sertraline and fluoxetine are licensed in children); clomipramine is second line. Benzodiazepines and antipsychotics are not first-line.

questions.question: An infant has marked hypotonia and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Which enzyme is defective?
questions.exp: Pompe disease (glycogen storage disease type II) is a lysosomal disorder: infantile form with floppy baby, big tongue, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (short PR, giant QRS on ECG), raised CK and no hypoglycaemia. Enzyme replacement (alglucosidase alfa) is available. G6Pase deficiency (type I) gives hypoglycaemia and a large liver; debrancher (type III) and McArdle (type V, muscle phosphorylase) are other GSDs.

questions.question: A 7-year-old boy has multiple café-au-lait patches and high blood pressure. What is the most likely cause of his hypertension?
questions.exp: Café-au-lait patches suggest neurofibromatosis type 1. In children with NF1 the most common cause of secondary hypertension is renal artery stenosis (fibromuscular dysplasia-like vasculopathy); phaeochromocytoma is less common in children. Measure BP yearly in all children with NF1, and image the renal arteries if raised.

questions.question: What is the most common inherited (single-gene) cause of intellectual disability?
questions.exp: Fragile X (CGG repeat expansion in FMR1 on Xq27.3, over 200 repeats) is the most common INHERITED cause of intellectual disability, and a common single-gene cause of autism. Boys: long face, large ears, macro-orchidism after puberty, hyperextensible joints, ADHD/autistic features. Down syndrome is the most common GENETIC (chromosomal) cause, but it is usually not inherited.

questions.question: A child with tetralogy of Fallot has a hypercyanotic spell. He has been put in the knee-chest position and given oxygen. What should be given next?
questions.exp: Tet spell steps: calm the child, knee-chest position (raises systemic resistance), oxygen, then morphine (IV/IM/intranasal) to reduce hyperpnoea and infundibular spasm, then a fluid bolus, IV propranolol or esmolol, sodium bicarbonate for acidosis, and phenylephrine to raise systemic resistance. Oral propranolol is used for prevention while awaiting surgery.

questions.question: A 9-year-old boy has just returned from a visit to an endemic area in South Asia. He has had high fever for 2 days with severe frontal and retro-orbital headache, muscle and joint pain and a flushed skin rash. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Dengue (Aedes mosquito, day-biting) causes sudden high fever, severe headache with retro-orbital pain, myalgia and arthralgia ("break-bone fever"), and a flushing or maculopapular rash, often with leucopenia and low platelets. Warning signs (abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding, rising haematocrit with falling platelets) usually appear around defervescence on days 3–7.

questions.question: The same child is seen on day 2 of fever. Which test best confirms dengue at this stage?
questions.exp: In the first 5 days of fever, the virus is in the blood: use RT-PCR (or NS1 antigen). Dengue IgM becomes positive from about day 5; IgG suggests past or secondary infection. Widal is for typhoid, and Monospot for EBV.

questions.question: What is the main mechanism behind severe dengue (dengue shock syndrome)?
questions.b: Plasma leakage from increased capillary permeability
questions.d: Direct invasion of the heart muscle
questions.exp: Severe dengue is caused by plasma leakage from capillaries, often linked to a second infection with a different serotype (antibody-dependent enhancement). It shows as a rising haematocrit, pleural effusions and ascites, low albumin and then shock, usually around the time the fever falls (critical phase). Treat with careful IV crystalloid guided by haematocrit and urine output.

questions.question: A child has a tender swollen lymph node in the axilla, 3 weeks after a kitten scratched his arm. Which organism is the cause?
questions.exp: Cat-scratch disease: a papule at the scratch site, then regional (often axillary or cervical) lymphadenopathy 1–3 weeks later, sometimes suppurating. Diagnosis is by Bartonella serology or PCR. Usually self-limiting; azithromycin speeds node resolution. Pasteurella causes rapid cellulitis within 24 hours of a cat or dog bite.

questions.question: A preterm baby born by vaginal delivery has an Apgar score of 9 at 5 minutes but develops tachypnoea and mild respiratory distress. What should be done first?
questions.a: Give surfactant by intubation straight away
questions.e: Give antibiotics only and observe in air
questions.exp: A spontaneously breathing preterm baby with respiratory distress should start on CPAP (European consensus guidelines): it reduces the need for intubation and bronchopulmonary dysplasia. Surfactant is given if oxygen needs rise (for example FiO2 above 0.30 on CPAP), preferably by a less invasive method (LISA). Blood cultures and antibiotics are also usually started in preterm babies with respiratory distress.

questions.question: A child has had cough and fever for 2 days. Examination shows reduced air entry and dullness to percussion at the left base. What is the expected radiological finding?
questions.e: Left lower lobe pneumonia with pleural effusion
questions.exp: Dullness to percussion with reduced air entry means fluid or consolidation; a "stony dull" base suggests a parapneumonic effusion with lower lobe pneumonia. Do an ultrasound to assess the fluid. A pneumothorax is hyper-resonant. A lung abscess is rare and shows a cavity with an air–fluid level.

questions.question: A term baby born through meconium-stained amniotic fluid develops respiratory distress and is admitted to the neonatal unit. What is the expected chest X-ray finding?
questions.a: Ground-glass appearance with air bronchograms and low lung volumes
questions.c: Small heart with a white-out of both lungs
questions.d: Coarse patchy infiltrates with hyperinflation (air trapping)
questions.e: Fluid in the horizontal fissure with clear lungs
questions.exp: Meconium aspiration syndrome: coarse, patchy, asymmetric infiltrates with areas of collapse and hyperinflation (ball-valve air trapping), and a risk of pneumothorax and persistent pulmonary hypertension. Ground-glass lungs with air bronchograms are RDS; fluid in the fissures is transient tachypnoea of the newborn.

questions.question: A 2-year-old girl has repeated attacks of fever lasting 1–3 days with arthritis, abdominal pain and a high white cell count. She is completely well between attacks. Her parents are cousins from the Middle East. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Familial Mediterranean fever (MEFV gene, autosomal recessive, common in Arab, Turkish, Armenian and Jewish people): short attacks (12–72 hours) of fever with serositis (peritonitis, pleurisy), arthritis or erysipelas-like rash, with high inflammatory markers that return to normal between attacks. Treat with daily colchicine to stop attacks and prevent amyloidosis.

questions.question: A 12-year-old girl has had a persistently raised ALT (100 U/L) on several visits, and she has iron deficiency anaemia. What should be done next?
questions.b: Repeat the liver function tests after 3 months
questions.d: Check anti-tissue transglutaminase IgA (with total IgA)
questions.exp: Coeliac disease commonly causes unexplained raised transaminases and iron deficiency anaemia, which do not respond to oral iron. Screen with anti-tTG IgA plus total IgA (IgA deficiency gives false negatives). The ALT usually returns to normal on a gluten-free diet. Liver biopsy is not a first step.

questions.question: An infant has clusters of flexor spasms, and the EEG shows hypsarrhythmia. Which drug is used for treatment?
questions.exp: Infantile spasms (West syndrome): spasms, hypsarrhythmia and developmental regression. First-line treatment is hormonal (prednisolone or ACTH) and/or vigabatrin; vigabatrin is first choice when the cause is tuberous sclerosis. Monitor visual fields (vigabatrin can cause field loss). Carbamazepine and phenytoin can make spasms worse.

questions.question: A child with seizures has an MRI showing subependymal nodules and a subependymal giant cell astrocytoma near the foramen of Monro. Which skin finding is associated with this condition?
questions.exp: Subependymal nodules and giant cell astrocytoma (SEGA) are typical of tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC1/TSC2). Skin signs: ash-leaf (hypomelanotic) macules, shagreen patch (thickened orange-peel skin over the lower back), facial angiofibromas, forehead plaque, periungual fibromas and confetti lesions. Café-au-lait spots and axillary freckling are NF1; port-wine stain is Sturge–Weber.

questions.question: A 4-day-old term baby is jaundiced. The mother is O positive and the baby is B positive with G6PD deficiency. The total serum bilirubin is 21 mg/dL (359 micromol/L). He is feeding well and neurologically normal. What is the best management?
questions.d: Intensive phototherapy, with close monitoring of bilirubin
questions.exp: Both ABO incompatibility and G6PD deficiency cause haemolysis and are neurotoxicity risk factors, so treatment thresholds are lower. At this level in a well, feeding baby, start intensive phototherapy, repeat the bilirubin in 4–6 hours, check the direct Coombs test, and prepare for exchange if it keeps rising or near the exchange line, or if there are signs of encephalopathy. IVIG is only for isoimmune haemolysis (Coombs positive) that keeps rising despite phototherapy; it does not help G6PD deficiency.

questions.question: A mother has children aged 6, 8 and 13 years and asks about a home trampoline. Which advice is correct?
questions.a: Somersaults are safe on a trampoline with a net enclosure
questions.b: A safety net prevents most injuries
questions.c: Trampolines carry no risk of neck or spinal injury
questions.d: Only one child should use the trampoline at a time, with adult supervision
questions.e: Several children can jump together safely if an adult watches
questions.exp: Most trampoline injuries happen when several children jump together, especially to the smallest child. The American Academy of Pediatrics discourages home trampolines; if used, only one jumper at a time, adult supervision, padding and a net, and no somersaults or flips (risk of cervical spine injury and paralysis). Nets do not prevent most injuries.

questions.question: A paediatric dentist needs to treat a dental abscess in a 5-year-old with mild developmental delay who cannot cooperate. What is the best approach to anaesthesia?
questions.a: General anaesthesia given by an anaesthetist
questions.b: Inhalational anaesthesia by the dentist alone, without IV access
questions.c: Postpone treatment until the child is older
questions.d: Oral sedation at home before the visit
questions.e: Local anaesthesia only, with the child held down
questions.exp: A child who cannot cooperate needs general anaesthesia, which must be given by a trained anaesthetist in a suitable setting with IV access and airway equipment, not by the operating dentist. Restraining a child for treatment or delaying treatment of an abscess is not acceptable.

questions.question: A 1-week-old boy is brought in with an apnoea. There was no fever and no infection in pregnancy. Examination shows a fracture of the 4th rib. What should be requested first?
questions.b: No tests; rib fractures are common after normal delivery
questions.exp: A rib fracture in a young infant, especially posterior, is highly specific for non-accidental injury (squeezing). An apparent life-threatening event may be from abusive head trauma or smothering. Start safeguarding: skeletal survey (repeated at 11–14 days), CT head, eye examination, and bloods for coagulation and bone chemistry. Birth-related rib fractures are rare and linked to difficult or large births.

questions.question: A child with sickle cell anaemia has a haemoglobin of 8 g/dL, with normal white cells and platelets, no splenomegaly and a bilirubin of 21 micromol/L. What should be requested?
questions.exp: A fall in haemoglobin in sickle cell disease needs a reticulocyte count first. A very LOW count suggests aplastic crisis (parvovirus B19, then send serology/PCR). A HIGH count with a big spleen suggests sequestration, or with jaundice suggests a haemolytic crisis. Hb electrophoresis only confirms the known diagnosis.

questions.question: A child with ADHD is starting methylphenidate. What should the mother be told?
questions.a: It may reduce appetite, so give it with or after breakfast and monitor growth
questions.b: It causes withdrawal, so it must never be stopped at weekends
questions.c: It increases appetite and weight gain
questions.d: It causes sleepiness, so give it at night
questions.e: It is safe to stop and start without any monitoring
questions.exp: Common side effects of methylphenidate: reduced appetite and weight loss, slowed growth, insomnia (give in the morning, not at night), headache, abdominal pain, tachycardia and raised BP. Monitor height, weight, pulse and BP. Planned breaks such as weekends or holidays are allowed and can help growth.

questions.question: A 13-year-old boy is short. His bone age is 10 years. He has no dysmorphic features and no other symptoms. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.c: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty
questions.exp: A delayed bone age in a healthy, normally proportioned boy with no other symptoms and a normal growth velocity suggests constitutional delay. Puberty and the growth spurt come late, but final height reaches the family target. In familial short stature the bone age matches the actual age. Check growth velocity; if it is low, look for GH deficiency or hypothyroidism.

questions.question: A child had an upper respiratory infection 2 weeks ago and now has ophthalmoplegia, areflexia and ataxia, and later weakness needing intubation. Which organism is most likely to have triggered this?
questions.exp: Ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and areflexia is the Miller Fisher variant of Guillain–Barré syndrome (anti-GQ1b antibodies), which can overlap with GBS and need ventilation. Infections that trigger GBS: Campylobacter jejuni (after diarrhoea, the most common overall), Mycoplasma pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae (after respiratory infections), CMV and EBV. Botulism causes a descending paralysis with fixed dilated pupils but no preceding infection.

questions.question: A 10 kg child has burns covering 40% of the body surface area. How much resuscitation fluid is needed in the first 8 hours (Parkland formula), in addition to maintenance fluid?
questions.exp: Parkland formula: 4 mL x weight (kg) x %TBSA burned = 4 x 10 x 40 = 1600 mL of Hartmann's over 24 hours from the time of the burn. Half (800 mL) is given in the first 8 hours, and half over the next 16 hours. Children also need maintenance fluid with glucose. Adjust to urine output (1 mL/kg/hour in children).

questions.question: A 7-year-old boy has signs of puberty. Both testes are 6 mL. Blood tests show high hCG, low LH and FSH, and testosterone in the pubertal range. What is the most likely cause?
questions.b: Leydig cell tumour of the testis
questions.d: An hCG-secreting germ cell tumour (peripheral precocious puberty)
questions.exp: hCG acts on LH receptors in the testes, causing testosterone production and modest bilateral testicular enlargement, while LH and FSH are suppressed (peripheral, gonadotrophin-independent puberty). Look for an hCG-secreting germ cell tumour in the brain (pineal or suprasellar), mediastinum or liver (hepatoblastoma). Central puberty has high LH and FSH; a Leydig cell tumour enlarges only one testis; CAH has small testes with raised 17-OHP.

questions.question: A boy has erythema nodosum. Which condition is it most likely to be associated with?
questions.exp: Erythema nodosum (tender red nodules on the shins) is a hypersensitivity reaction. Causes in children: streptococcal infection (most common), TB, inflammatory bowel disease (more with Crohn's disease, and often parallels disease activity), sarcoidosis, drugs and EBV. Coeliac disease is linked to dermatitis herpetiformis instead.

questions.question: A 5-year-old boy with hepatitis B presents with foetor hepaticus, asterixis and a prolonged prothrombin time. Which statement is true?
questions.a: Liver enzymes always stay very high as the disease worsens
questions.b: The ammonia level closely matches the severity of encephalopathy
questions.c: Vitamin K will correct the prothrombin time
questions.d: A metabolic acidosis with a respiratory alkalosis can occur
questions.e: Protein must be stopped completely for several days
questions.exp: Acute liver failure: encephalopathy and coagulopathy (INR not corrected by vitamin K, because the liver cannot make clotting factors). Central hyperventilation causes respiratory alkalosis, and lactic acidosis causes metabolic acidosis. Ammonia correlates poorly with the grade of encephalopathy (though very high levels predict cerebral oedema). Falling transaminases with rising bilirubin and INR is a bad sign (liver cells running out). Refer to a liver transplant centre.

questions.question: A child with large adenoids snores, breathes through the mouth and has poor concentration at school. What should be done?
questions.a: Give a course of oral antibiotics
questions.b: Reassure; it will settle by itself
questions.c: Refer to a psychologist for behaviour therapy
questions.e: Refer to ENT for assessment for adenotonsillectomy
questions.exp: Snoring, mouth breathing and daytime poor concentration, hyperactivity or sleepiness suggest obstructive sleep apnoea from adenotonsillar hypertrophy. Refer to ENT; adenotonsillectomy is the main treatment. Polysomnography confirms OSA when the picture is unclear or before surgery in high-risk children. Do not label it ADHD before treating the sleep problem.

questions.question: A child was under water for a few minutes. He is now alert, with normal vital signs and no symptoms. What should be done?
questions.a: Give steroids to prevent lung injury
questions.e: Admit to intensive care and intubate
questions.exp: After a drowning incident, a child who is well may still develop lung injury (pulmonary oedema, ARDS) over the next hours. Observe for at least 6–8 hours with oxygen saturations and a chest examination; discharge if normal. Prophylactic antibiotics and steroids are not recommended.

questions.question: After a pancreatectomy, a child has severe pain despite regular paracetamol and tramadol. What is the best next step?
questions.a: Intramuscular morphine every 4 hours as needed
questions.c: Intravenous opioid by patient-controlled analgesia (for example morphine PCA)
questions.e: Increase the tramadol dose above the maximum
questions.exp: Severe pain after major abdominal surgery needs a strong opioid (step 3 of the WHO ladder), ideally IV by patient- or nurse-controlled analgesia, with regular paracetamol and monitoring of sedation and breathing. IM injections are painful and give uneven levels. Codeine is not recommended in children (variable metabolism).

questions.question: An unvaccinated child has fever for 3 days and an itchy vesicular rash on the trunk and chest. How is this infection spread?
questions.b: Airborne droplets and direct contact with the vesicle fluid
questions.exp: Chickenpox (varicella-zoster virus) spreads by airborne/respiratory droplets and direct contact with fluid from the blisters. It is infectious from 1–2 days before the rash until all lesions have crusted (about 5 days). Incubation is 10–21 days. Lesions appear in crops (papules, vesicles and crusts together), mostly on the trunk.

questions.question: A newborn baby is diagnosed with very long-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (VLCAD) deficiency. What dietary advice is correct?
questions.c: Corn starch only with a fat-free diet
questions.d: Restrict long-chain fat and give medium-chain triglyceride (MCT) supplements, avoiding fasting
questions.exp: VLCAD deficiency is a fatty acid oxidation defect: the body cannot use long-chain fats for energy during fasting. It causes hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, cardiomyopathy, liver dysfunction and rhabdomyolysis. Management: avoid fasting (frequent feeds, emergency glucose regimen when ill), restrict long-chain fats, and give MCT oil, which bypasses the block.

questions.question: An 18-month-old child is told off and starts crying. He then stops breathing, turns blue, goes limp for a few seconds and recovers fully. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Cyanotic breath-holding spells (6 months to 5 years) are triggered by anger or frustration: crying, breath held in expiration, cyanosis, then brief loss of tone or a few jerks, with quick full recovery. Reflex anoxic seizures (pallid spells) follow a sudden painful bump, with pallor from vagal asystole. Reassure; check for iron deficiency.

questions.question: A toddler has recurrent cyanotic breath-holding spells with brief jerking of both arms after the attack; in the last one he fell to the ground. Which test is most useful?
questions.exp: Breath-holding spells are a clinical diagnosis; the brief jerks are anoxic, not epileptic, so EEG and MRI are not needed. Iron deficiency anaemia is common in these children, and iron treatment reduces the attacks even without anaemia, so check FBC and ferritin. An ECG is advised if attacks are atypical, without a trigger, or with exercise or a family history of sudden death (to exclude long QT).

questions.question: A newborn has jaundice, a severe coagulopathy and hepatomegaly. Which test confirms the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Tyrosinaemia type 1 (fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase deficiency) causes early liver failure with a coagulopathy out of proportion to other liver tests, renal Fanconi syndrome, rickets and a high risk of hepatocellular carcinoma. Raised succinylacetone in urine or blood is diagnostic; tyrosine is raised in many liver diseases, so it is not specific. Treat with nitisinone and a low tyrosine and phenylalanine diet.

questions.question: A 14-year-old boy has scrotal pain after a minor injury. Examination shows a small blue dot at the upper pole of the testis, and the testis itself is not tender. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.c: Torsion of the testicular appendage (hydatid of Morgagni)
questions.exp: The "blue dot sign" is a twisted, infarcted appendix testis seen through the scrotal skin, with tenderness limited to the upper pole and a normal cremasteric reflex. It is managed with rest and analgesia. If testicular torsion cannot be excluded clinically, explore surgically without delay (the testis can be lost within 6 hours).

questions.question: A 3-year-old had a high fever for 4 days, treated with paracetamol and ibuprofen. As the fever settled, a pink maculopapular rash appeared on the trunk. He is well and playing. What should be done?
questions.a: Stop paracetamol and ibuprofen because of a drug reaction
questions.exp: Roseola infantum (HHV-6, sometimes HHV-7): several days of high fever in a well child (febrile convulsions can occur), then, as the fever falls, a pink, non-itchy maculopapular rash on the trunk. It is self-limiting; reassure. A rash that appears after the fever settles is the clue that it is not a drug allergy.

questions.question: A short girl has a Madelung deformity of the wrist on X-ray. Which gene is most likely to be affected?
questions.exp: A SHOX gene defect causes Léri–Weill dyschondrosteosis: short stature with short forearms and lower legs (mesomelia) and Madelung deformity (bowing of the radius with dorsal dislocation of the ulna), more marked in girls. SHOX loss also explains the short stature in Turner syndrome. Growth hormone treatment is licensed. FGFR3 is achondroplasia, COL1A1 osteogenesis imperfecta, FBN1 Marfan and PTPN11 Noonan.

questions.question: A child in status epilepticus has had two doses of a benzodiazepine (midazolam) and is still fitting. What should be given next?
questions.c: Rapid sequence induction with thiopentone straight away
questions.exp: After two doses of benzodiazepine, give a second-line drug: IV levetiracetam 40 mg/kg or phenytoin 20 mg/kg over 20 minutes (APLS/NICE 2022). If the seizure continues, give the other second-line drug, then rapid sequence induction with an anaesthetist about 45 minutes in. More than two benzodiazepine doses increases respiratory depression.

questions.question: A child has a round patch of hair loss on the scalp. The skin is smooth, not scaly, swollen or red. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Alopecia areata: well-defined round patches of complete hair loss with smooth, normal skin and "exclamation mark" hairs at the edge (autoimmune). Tinea capitis gives scaly patches with broken hairs; a kerion is a boggy, swollen, inflamed mass. Telogen effluvium causes diffuse thinning 2–3 months after a stress. Trichotillomania gives irregular patches with hairs of different lengths.

questions.question: A mother with sickle cell disease was given morphine during the last 2 weeks of pregnancy. After a traumatic delivery, the baby had low Apgar scores and a cord pH of 7.12 and was given naloxone. The baby then developed seizures. What is the most likely cause of the seizures?
questions.b: Acute opioid withdrawal precipitated by naloxone
questions.exp: Naloxone must NOT be given to babies of mothers on long-term opioids, because it can trigger sudden withdrawal with seizures. Here the mother had 2 weeks of morphine. A cord pH of 7.12 is only mild acidosis (HIE usually needs a pH under 7.0), so the seizure timing after naloxone points to withdrawal. Support breathing with ventilation instead.
